title: You can skip the crisis, but you can’t skip the midlife
author: Molly Graham
summary: Molly Graham uses her WorkLife podcast conversation with Chip Conley, founder of the Modern Elder Academy, to ask whether ambition has seasons and whether midlife must be a crisis. She frames the question through her own story of reaching the big job she had chased for twenty years and discovering she no longer wanted it. The piece distills three takeaways: the reckoning of midlife is unavoidable even if the crisis is optional, curiosity works as a compass when direction is unclear, and purpose should be managed as a portfolio rather than a single dominant slice. Graham stresses Conley's idea of transitional intelligence, especially the neglected work of marking endings with real rituals. She also records his practical answer to the objection that reinvention is a luxury: meet your obligations first, then start the other thing anyway. The essay ends with Conley's reflections on living with a cancer diagnosis and holding holy urgency and slowing down together.
points: Conley's concept of transitional intelligence asks leaders to recognize whether they are at an ending, a middle, or a beginning, because each stage demands something different.
Graham argues that most people skip the ending, and that you cannot start something new while still half-attached to what is over.
When curiosity feels absent, Conley's forcing question is what you will regret not learning or doing ten years from now.
The purpose portfolio idea treats midlife as a rebalancing act: dose down what has become too dominant, often work, and dose up what gives purpose.
quotes: I spent the first 20 years of my career chasing one definition of success - a big impact in a big job - and proving I could get there. Then I did... and found I didn't want it anymore.
Chip is emphatic that he would have changed his life even without his near-death experience - it just would have taken longer. The crisis is optional; the reckoning isn't.
The part most of us skip is the ending. You can't start something new while you're still half-attached to the thing that's over, and we've built almost no way to mark that in this culture.
He put it this way: talented people deserve empty space. If you have talent and curiosity, you're good soil, and something will grow - even if you can't name it yet.
Chip talked about purpose as a pie chart, and most of us let one slice take over the whole thing - for me it was work, for years, and it was genuinely enough until it wasn't.
First, be a responsible adult - get your obligations in order, don't blow anything up. Second, once that's handled, start the other thing anyway.
